notes.meaning: Work on the temple had stopped for about fifteen years, and the people had grown discouraged and focused only on their own homes. God sent two prophets, Haggai and Zechariah, to remind the people that the Lord was still with them and wanted His house rebuilt. Their preaching stirred the hearts of the returned exiles to turn back to the work. When we drift away from God's work, His word calls us to wake up and start fresh.

Zerubbabel the civic governor and Jeshua the high priest responded immediately to the preaching and went back to work on the temple. The prophets did not just speak from a distance; they stood alongside the builders, offering continuous encouragement and practical help. Good leaders lead by taking action, especially when encouraged by the truth of God.

A Persian governor named Tattenai arrived to inspect the construction taking place in Jerusalem. Because the Persian empire had recently faced revolts, he wanted to know who gave the Jews official permission to rebuild such a large structure. Unlike earlier enemies who used violence, this governor was carrying out a calm and routine investigation.

Tattenai and his officials asked for the names of the men in charge of the building project. They wanted a written record of the leaders so they could hold specific people responsible if this work turned out to be an illegal revolt. The Jewish leaders answered openly, having nothing to hide because they knew they were doing God's work.

The phrase "the eye of their God" describes the Lord's watchful care and protection over His people. Instead of shutting down the project immediately, the Persian officials allowed the builders to keep working while they sent a letter to King Darius. God guided the minds of these rulers so that His work could continue without another long delay.

Tattenai and his fellow inspectors wrote a formal letter to King Darius in Persia. This written record was preserved and copied into the book of Ezra. Unlike earlier letters from hostile neighbors, this report aimed to be an honest and balanced account of the situation.

The letter opened with the standard Persian royal greeting, wishing the king total peace and well-being. This polite and respectful tone showed that the officials were following proper legal channels. It set the stage for an orderly report about the events in Jerusalem.

The officials reported that the temple of the God of Judah was being rebuilt with heavy stones and wooden beams inside the walls, a common method to protect against earthquakes. They also noted that the builders were working hard and making rapid progress. Even though the officials did not worship Israel's God, they recognized the seriousness and importance of the work.

In their letter, the officials explained to the king how they questioned the Jewish elders on site. They asked the builders to show what authority or royal order gave them the right to construct the building. This fair reporting gave King Darius the exact context of the investigation.

Tattenai reported that he asked for the names of the men leading the project so the king would know who was responsible. Gathering names was standard Persian procedure to maintain imperial order. It shows that the officials were being thorough rather than cruel.

The Jewish elders began their answer by declaring their loyalty to the God who created everything in heaven and on earth. They explained that they were not starting a new rebellion, but restoring an ancient temple built centuries before by King Solomon. They shared their faith boldly, showing honor to God before royal officials.

The elders honestly admitted that the temple lay in ruins because their ancestors had sinned and provoked God's judgment. God used Nebuchadnezzar, the Babylonian king, as His tool to punish them and take them into exile. Taking responsibility for past sin gave their testimony great honesty and moral strength.

The elders explained that after the Babylonian empire fell, King Cyrus of Persia conquered Babylon and issued an official decree. Cyrus gave the Jewish people royal permission to return home and rebuild the temple. This decree gave them full legal authority under Persian law to do what they were doing.

Cyrus also returned the sacred gold and silver cups and plates that Nebuchadnezzar had stolen from the temple decades earlier. The king placed these valuable treasures into the hands of Sheshbazzar, whom he had appointed as governor of Judah. Returning these sacred items proved that the Persian crown had fully supported the restoration.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern commentators view Sheshbazzar as a distinct Persian-appointed official who led the first return, rather than another name for Zerubbabel.

notes.meaning: Cyrus gave direct orders for the sacred vessels to be brought back to Jerusalem and placed in the rebuilt temple. The decree specified that the new temple had to be constructed on its exact original location. The Jewish elders cited these specific commands to prove they were simply carrying out royal orders.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern commentators view Sheshbazzar as a distinct Persian-appointed official who led the first return, rather than another name for Zerubbabel.

notes.meaning: Sheshbazzar obeyed the royal command, traveled to Jerusalem, and laid the foundations of the temple. The elders stated that the work had continued on and off since that time, which explained why it was still not finished. They presented their building project as one ongoing effort authorized by Cyrus, rather than a new and rebellious venture.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars often view Sheshbazzar as an earlier Persian-appointed leader who laid the initial groundwork, distinguishing him from Zerubbabel, who led the later rebuilding effort.

notes.meaning: Tattenai concluded his letter by asking King Darius to search the royal archives in Babylon for the original decree of Cyrus. He did not tell the king what to decide, but simply asked for instructions once the records were found. Trusting God often allows us to be completely open and unafraid of the truth.
